strategy_title: Autotune larger XBLOCK to eliminate partial wave
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512–2048) to eliminate a partial wave caused a regression because the larger tile sizes forced the compiler to allocate more registers per thread (29→38), which reduced Block Limit Registers from 16 to 12 and dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 76.5% to 61.1%. The increased register pressure also caused a 66% increase in executed instructions (2.86M→4.75M), overwhelming any benefit from eliminating the partial wave tail. When the kernel is already register-constrained near the occupancy ceiling, increasing XBLOCK inflates register pressure and causes a net slowdown despite reducing grid size.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: small XBLOCK, high occupancy, low register pressure
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    # ... kernel body ...

grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # 4900 blocks, 29 regs/thread, 100% theoretical occupancy
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Kernel has a partial wave (waves_per_sm is non-integer with significant fractional part), low register usage per thread (well below 32), and theoretical occupancy is already at 100% with headroom in Block Limit Registers.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is already near register budget limits (registers_per_thread >= 28–32); increasing XBLOCK will inflate register pressure, reduce Block Limit Registers, drop theoretical and achieved occupancy, and increase total instruction count — causing a net regression even if grid size is reduced. Also avoid when the kernel body contains many live variables that scale with XBLOCK tile size.
framework_notes: In Triton, larger XBLOCK values cause the compiler to keep more intermediate values live simultaneously (e.g., loaded tiles, intermediate computations), increasing register pressure. This is distinct from CUDA where tile size and register usage are more decoupled. The autotune overhead itself is not the cause — the regression is purely from the register pressure increase at the selected larger XBLOCK.

strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK upward to eliminate partial-wave tail
strategy_description: Adding triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512/1024/2048) to eliminate a partial-wave tail caused register pressure to increase from 29 to 38 registers/thread. This dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% (Block Limit Registers fell from 16 to 12 blocks/SM) and achieved occupancy from 76.5% to 60.8%. The autotune overhead also inflated the executed instruction count by ~66% (2.86M to 4.75M), and the kernel duration increased from 7.26 µs to 9.86 µs — a 36% regression. The partial-wave tail savings were completely offset by the occupancy loss from register spill.
slow_pseudocode:
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # 29 registers/thread, 100% theoretical occupancy
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    ...
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Never — this specific combination caused regression. In general, increasing XBLOCK via autotune may help when: registers/thread are low (<24), theoretical occupancy is already below 100% and register-limited, and the partial-wave tail is the dominant bottleneck.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already uses close to 29+ registers/thread and achieves 100% theoretical occupancy. Increasing XBLOCK in such kernels raises register pressure, reduces Block Limit Registers, drops theoretical and achieved occupancy, and increases total instruction count — all of which worsen latency. Also note: if the launch grid is not updated to use meta['XBLOCK'] (lambda grid), the autotune XBLOCK change has no effect on grid size, defeating the purpose.
framework_notes: Critical implementation flaw observed: the kernel_function still used a fixed grid=(cdiv(xnumel, 128),) instead of a lambda grid using meta['XBLOCK']. This means the grid size did not shrink even though autotune selected larger XBLOCK values, so the partial-wave benefit was never realized. The autotune overhead (extra instruction count from autotuning passes) and register pressure increase were the only effects. In Triton, autotune with variable XBLOCK requires: grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
